name: Milk thistle (silymarin)
short: One case report of raised INR on warfarin. Nausea and diarrhoea are reported; pooled trials found little or no difference in serious adverse events (low certainty). Caution in pregnancy advised.
text: A safety review reports that silymarin is safe in humans at therapeutic doses, with some gastrointestinal discomfort such as nausea and diarrhoea, and no major toxicity in animals, although it was mutagenic in one bacterial test in the presence of metabolic enzymes; the review advises caution during pregnancy, noting that a single clinical trial found no anomalies and that more human studies are needed. A systematic review of 17 randomised trials in 2069 adults with fatty liver disease covered silymarin alone (nine trials) and silymarin complexes (eight trials); for silymarin alone compared with placebo or no intervention, it found that there may be little or no difference in serious adverse events (Peto odds ratio 1.55, 95% CI 0.26 to 9.28; 4 trials, 304 participants; low-certainty evidence) and that the evidence on non-serious adverse events was very uncertain (risk ratio 1.29, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.89; 4 trials, 282 participants; very low-certainty evidence); one trial reported serious adverse events, none judged related to the study drugs, and the authors concluded that the benefits and harms are unclear. On interactions, a systematic review of pharmacokinetic studies found that most human studies showed no silymarin-drug interactions, with more interactions seen in animal studies at much higher doses, and the safety review says it has no major effects on cytochrome P-450 enzymes but should be used with caution alongside drugs with a narrow therapeutic window. A single case report describes a man well controlled on warfarin whose INR rose from 2.64 to 4.12 after he started a supplement containing milk thistle and returned to normal after he stopped it; the abstract does not say what else the supplement contained.
